title: Capacity planning, latency & AI economics
summary: Estimate memory and workload cost with explicit assumptions and measurements.
html:
Estimate memory and workload cost with explicit assumptions and measurements.

Begin with a workload definition

Record input/output lengths, concurrency, arrival pattern, model, precision, and quality constraints. A tokens-per-second number without these settings is not a portable performance claim. Prefill and decoding exercise hardware differently, and aggregate throughput can improve while individual latency worsens.

Count all memory

Inference needs weights, KV cache, activations, workspaces, allocator overhead, and the runtime. Training adds gradients and optimizer state. Quantization metadata and temporary dequantization can reduce expected savings. Sharding distributes some allocations while introducing communication and per-device overhead.

Separate peak from useful capacity

Peak arithmetic is a theoretical ceiling under specified operations. Sustained performance depends on kernel shape, memory traffic, links, and occupancy. Reserve capacity for bursts and failures. A service operating at maximum utilization may develop unacceptable tail latency.

Compare cost at equal quality

Compute cost per accepted task or useful output, not just raw tokens. Include retries, evaluator calls, retrieval, storage, networking, engineering, and human review where applicable. Electricity equals power integrated over time; chip TDP is not a measurement of total facility consumption.

Worked example

A job using eight GPUs for three hours consumes 24 GPU-hours. At an explicitly assumed rate of 2 currency units per GPU-hour, accelerator rental alone is 48 units. This is a scenario calculation, not a current price quote; add the rest of the system’s costs.

What goes wrong

Comparing a sparse FP4 headline against dense BF16 throughput conflates precision and sparsity. Cost numbers expire as workloads, prices, and implementations change.

Check your understanding

Can maximizing batch size harm a user-facing service?

Reveal the explanation

Yes. Waiting to fill batches or processing larger batches can increase per-request latency even if total throughput rises.

How the pieces connect

A usable chapter has a flow of decisions, evidence, and checks. Use this diagram as a navigation aid, then test each step on a small real example.

An operating model for capacity planning, latency & ai economics

Capacity planning converts a vague performance goal into explicit tradeoffs. A service can increase total throughput by batching while making individual responses slower; a cheaper numerical format can reduce cost while changing quality; a larger memory pool can prevent failures while increasing idle spend.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Field guide: four decisions in order

1. Define demand

Define demand establishes the next constraint. Specify arrival rate, concurrency, quality, and latency target. Begin by making the object of study explicit. A vague input, target, or operating condition creates ambiguity that later computation cannot repair.

Write down the input boundary and the unit of analysis. This makes it possible to distinguish a missing fact from a mismatch between the question and the data or system.

2. Model resources

Model resources establishes the next constraint. Count memory, compute, links, storage, and queue capacity. Now make the mechanism inspectable. Prefer a small run whose intermediate values, examples, or traces can be examined before you automate a larger workflow.

Keep a concrete artifact: a small dataset, a notebook cell, a trace, a benchmark command, or a hand-worked calculation. It is the fastest way to surface hidden assumptions.

3. Measure utilization

Measure utilization establishes the next constraint. Observe saturation and tail latency under load. Treat the first result as a measurement, not a conclusion. Compare it with a baseline and vary one assumption at a time so that the observed change has an interpretable cause.

Check a deliberately awkward case alongside the happy path. Boundary conditions, rare examples, and resource limits reveal more than another aggregate score.

4. Choose policy

Choose policy establishes the next constraint. Set batching, limits, autoscaling, and fallback behavior. Finish by connecting the result to a real choice. Record the operating range, uncertainty, and the condition under which the next person should stop, escalate, or revisit the earlier steps.

Preserve the decision record with the result. A useful technical chapter leaves enough context for a reader to reproduce the reasoning, challenge it, and choose a safe next action.

When the first approach fails

Do not respond to a weak result by immediately adding scale, complexity, or another framework. First locate the failure: the input may not match the intended problem; the representation may discard a useful signal; the measurement may reward the wrong outcome; or the system may have crossed a memory, latency, reliability, or authority boundary. Change one layer, repeat the smallest useful check, and keep the before-and-after evidence.

Gotcha. A polished output can hide an untested assumption. The most convincing demonstration is a counterexample the workflow handles deliberately, with the limitation stated in the release or research record.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Define demand. Specify arrival rate, concurrency, quality, and latency target.
  2. Model resources. Count memory, compute, links, storage, and queue capacity.
  3. Measure utilization. Observe saturation and tail latency under load.
  4. Choose policy. Set batching, limits, autoscaling, and fallback behavior.

Run a load test with realistic prompt lengths and burst patterns. Report admission behavior, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, memory peak, error rate, and cost per accepted result.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
